title: Planned my quad rows around this handle, and the inside bend still pinches
author: med_yasss
selftext:
This cleanup started with an image-based wrench prop for my game, a hand tool with a thick curved handle. My goal was a topology layout I could edit around the curve while keeping the silhouette. In Blender, I planned broad quad rows across quiet surfaces and a gradual density transition where the handle joins the head.



The initial image-to-3D base mesh came from a reference photo I processed in meshy. From there, the retopology and edge-flow choices were mine. Along the inner curve of the handle, I tested a triangle fan to carry the denser junction into the simpler shaft. With the viewport light spinning, that layout pinched. Redirecting those diagonals into uneven quads made the highlight look lumpy, while adding loops pushed the density back up around a spot that will barely move.



My failed attempt was rebuilding that patch as an all-quad grid. I got cleaner rows, but I also flattened the inner curve and lost the chunky shape from the reference.



Would you leave that triangle fan on a static prop, or rebuild it?

comments.author: rudrathegoat2204
comments.body: I ran into a similar bend on a curved grip. I let meshy do the remesh pass first, kept most of that layout, and rebuilt only the junction in Blender, adding two gradual transition rings before the simpler shaft. Sliding a light across it, the abrupt density change showed more than the triangle fan itself.

replies.author: -WarDaddy-29
replies.body: Those transition rings should help. I?d still keep an eye on where the five-edge poles settle, because one on the inside bend can bunch the shading even with an all-quad patch. Moving that pole toward the flatter side of the handle usually gives the curve more room to absorb the density change.

comments.author: Lopsided_Heat_7455
comments.body: Transition rings help, although I would watch where the five-edge poles land. A pole on the inside bend can bunch the shading even when every face is a quad. Sliding it toward the flatter side of the handle usually gives the curve more room to carry the change.
